title: Westbrook City Council — Committee of the Whole

fields.Time: 7:00 PM (immediately following the Regular meeting and executive session)
fields.Location: Westbrook High School (Room 114), 125 Stroudwater St. (Hybrid via Zoom)

note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. This Committee of the Whole session and the Regular City Council meeting that preceded it the same night share this one video recording; this summary covers only the Committee of the Whole portion, which began roughly 45 minutes after the Regular meeting recessed into executive session. See the separate September 14, 2026 Regular Meeting summary for the first part of the evening. For complete context, nuance, and anything not covered here, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Present: Chair Gary Rairdon, President Jennifer Munro, Vice President Michael Shaughnessy, Victor Chau, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham. Absent: Brian McCambridge.

blocks.x: Call to Order & Referral of July 20 Items
Housekeeping Referral: Four Boards Reviewed July 20 Formally Sent to Council
Discussion Summary

Councilor Gary Rairdon opened the session. He said he is Chair of the Committee of the Whole, a different role from the City Council Presidency (held by President Munro). Roll call: six of seven members present (Councilor McCambridge absent).
This was the second of at least three planned sessions reviewing the City's comprehensive overhaul of its ordinance (a city law) on boards, commissions and committees. The review began July 20, 2026.

Before taking up tonight's new items, the Committee noted that four boards reviewed July 20 had never actually been formally referred to City Council for final adoption. They are the Board of Assessment Review, Board of Trustees of Woodlawn Cemetery, Fair Hearing Authority, and Library Advisory Committee. A motion tonight fixed this oversight.
Key Decisions
Motion to refer all four July 20 items to City Council passed by unanimous roll call, 6–0. Moved by Jennifer Munro. Seconder not stated on the recording.
Action Items
None.
Public Safety Commission — Review Tabled

Before staff could present their findings on the Public Safety Commission, Commission Chair Mike Fandel spoke briefly. The commission was planned for review tonight alongside three other boards. He said he'd met with City staff that afternoon to share his concerns and would continue that dialogue.

Commission Secretary Dustin Slate was unable to attend in person. He submitted a detailed written comment, which City Clerk Ellis Ledoux read into the record. It raised three specific compliance concerns that the draft ordinance amendment did not address:

“Section 80-3 of the Code requires the Public Safety Commission to draft, adopt, and publish rules governing how police, fire, and communication employees are hired and promoted... that documentation simply does not exist... [Section 80-6] says that only the Commission ‘shall keep records of its proceedings’... there is no formal workflow on how these records are created, retained, or made available... in my opinion, the city is currently in violation of Maine Freedom of Access Act.”
blocks.cite: Dustin Slate, Secretary, Public Safety Commission (letter read into the record)

blocks.x: Slate's letter also flagged a third issue. Section 80-7 requires 24-hour advance public notice for Commission business, and he said that notice is not being posted. In his opinion, this is another point on which the city is out of compliance with the Freedom of Access Act. He asked that the ordinance review address all three issues rather than let them persist through another review cycle.
Key Decisions

Motion to table (set aside to take up later) the Public Safety Commission portion of tonight's review [1:56:45] passed by unanimous roll call, 6–0. This gives staff time to add this feedback before returning with a revised proposal. Moved by Jennifer Munro, seconded by Victor Chau.
Zoning Board of Appeals
Enforcement Appeals Routed to Court; Shoreland Zoning Inconsistency Fixed
Found on page 12 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

Assistant City Administrator Jennie Franceschi presented staff's findings. The board's purpose, five-member-plus-two-alternate structure, and duties were all found clear and appropriate, with no changes proposed.

Most of the amendment deals with scope of authority, on legal counsel's recommendation. Enforcement actions by the Code Enforcement Officer would no longer be appealable to the Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA). Violators would instead seek remedy through the courts. This is meant to address costly litigation.
Appeals of the Officer's ordinance interpretations and permit decisions would still go to the ZBA. This change touches many ordinance chapters:
Building Construction
Electrical Standards
Fire Protection
Stormwater Management
Streets and Sidewalks
Weapons and Explosives
Land Use
Separately, “shall” language that could be read to require immediate enforcement would be amended. That preserves the City's preference for voluntary compliance.

A related fix corrects an inconsistency the ZBA's own chair flagged. Appeals of Planning Board decisions on Shoreland Zoning Permits currently go to the ZBA. Every other Planning Board appeal goes to court. This amendment aligns Shoreland Zoning with that standard practice.

Councilor Turcotte raised a related question. Current ordinance language bars a sitting councilor's spouse from serving on the ZBA, which is a Maine statutory requirement. No equivalent restriction exists for the Planning Board, where her own husband currently serves.

City Solicitor Cameron Ferrante confirmed that the state requires the ZBA restriction but not the Planning Board one. Ferrante agreed to research whether the City should apply a consistent standard across both bodies.

Discussion also touched on why ward-specific seat requirements have been removed citywide over time. The aim was to ease recruitment and staffing. A past Public Safety Commission vacancy illustrated this: it went unfilled for roughly two years before a ward requirement was dropped.
Key Decisions
Referred to City Council for consideration by unanimous roll call, 6–0. Motion and second by Jennifer Munro and Victor Chau; the chair named both without saying which seconded.
Action Items
None.
Planning Board
Scope Cleanup; Removal Procedure & Alternate-Voting Q&A
Found on page 30 of the packet.
Discussion Summary
Franceschi reported that the board's purpose, seven-member-plus-two-alternate size, and duties were all found appropriate. The scope-of-authority section needed updating.

It had outdated language suggesting the Planning Board has authority over fee-setting, contracts, budget management, or Capital Improvement Program decisions. Those functions conflict with the City Charter. The board does not actually perform them.

Clerical cleanup includes addressing gendered language. It also extends the required report-back period to Council from 60 to a 90-day minimum. It removes an unnecessary savings provision and outdated public-records language.

Councilor Chau asked why the Planning Board alone has an explicit removal procedure, which requires Mayor action sustained by a two-thirds Council vote, when other boards don't specify one [2:14:04]. Staff explained that the ZBA's removal process (and its spousal restriction) comes directly from state statute. The Planning Board's removal process isn't covered by state law, so it needed explicit ordinance language. Staff said the higher threshold reflects the board's more highly political role.
Chau also asked about alternates' voting rights. That prompted a separate explainer: all seven voting members' votes count officially even when alternates take full part in discussion.

Councilor Turcotte suggested the ordinance could explicitly empower board members to flag a colleague for removal “for cause”, rather than leaving that authority only with the Mayor and Council [2:19:31]. Her example was a hypothetical member who stopped paying city taxes. Staff agreed to review the wording.
Key Decisions
Referred to City Council for consideration by unanimous roll call, 6–0. Moved by Jennifer Munro, seconded by Victor Chau.
Action Items
None.
Village Review Overlay Zone (VROZ) Committee — Recommended for Elimination
Committee Sunset Recommended; Design Standards Continue Under the Planning Board
Found on page 36 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

This three-member advisory committee reviews downtown development proposals against the City's Village Review Overlay Zone architectural standards. It began informally some time after the Village Review Overlay Zone was created in 2007. It was formally written into the ordinance as a Planning Board advisory body in 2019.

Franceschi gave a lot of history. The committee's original purpose was to encourage (not mandate) architectural quality in downtown redevelopment. That came before the specific VROZ standards eventually adopted in 2017.

Along the way, the committee was also inserted into the City's demolition-delay ordinance. This inadvertently created a long permitting process for routine, non-historic demolitions (garages, sheds, blighted structures). That was a flaw in the ordinance's drafting, not the committee's fault.

Staff's recommendation: end (sunset) the VROZ Committee as a standalone body. Planning Board review of downtown projects has grown significantly more detailed over the past decade. It now duplicates much of what the VROZ Committee does.
Meanwhile, the committee itself has dwindled to one or two meetings a year. They are conducted by Zoom at an early-morning time chosen for members' convenience, with limited public accessibility.

Under the proposed changes, the architectural standards themselves would remain fully in effect, enforced directly by the Planning Board and staff. Demolition permits would require formal review only for structures listed or eligible for the National Register of Historic Places.

Councilor Chau asked several clarifying questions distinguishing the VROZ Committee (being eliminated) from the VROZ standards (continuing under Planning Board review) [2:31:37]. He also asked what staff heard from the committee's own members when the sunset idea was raised. Staff said no one welcomes news like that, but described a really great conversation. Staff said members felt parts of the standards need updating, and staff would like to bring them in on that work.

Councilor Michael Shaughnessy voiced support. He noted that moving review to the Planning Board level should strengthen community input, since public participation is already an established part of the process there. He described the review as often subjective and aesthetics-driven.
Key Decisions
Referred to City Council for consideration by unanimous roll call, 6–0. Motion and second by Jennifer Munro and Victor Chau; the chair named both without saying which seconded.
Action Items
None.
Closing
Staff Thanked, Meeting Adjourned
Discussion Summary

Chair Rairdon thanked staff for their work on the review of boards, commissions and committees. He noted that tonight's referrals will be taken up for final consideration by the full City Council. No further business; meeting adjourned.
Key Decisions
Motion to adjourn approved. Motion and second by Anna Turcotte and Jennifer Munro; the chair named both without saying which seconded.
Action Items
None.
